# **The Bay Tribune Daily News — Cycle 112**

---

### **The Edition’s Stories by Reporter**

#### **Mobility, Mentions, and the City’s Buzz**
*By Celeste Tran, Bay Tribune Wire*

West Oakland drew the largest share of new arrivals in Cycle 112, with **18 residents** shifting in while musician **Jade Orion’s** media mentions ticked up to 18 total [1]. Across town in Rockridge, **Yu Zen** caught the changing pace during morning walks, noting new faces and music drifting from apartments, adding that his family loves seeing the city fill up with new creative energy [1]. 

Living near Lake Merritt, **Jade Orion** shrugged off her rising count, keeping her focus on her music while neighborhood volunteers from the Cathedral of the Living Word continued street cleanups [2]. Journalist **Tara Ellison**, whose mentions reached 12, observed local film crews near the Rockridge waterfront while noting that *Tribune* management recently asked her to redo previously approved work [3]. Meanwhile, A's legend **Vinnie Keane** pointed to strong community energy at an Or Hashalom Renewal Community health fair, observing how neighborhood residents continue to rally around the team [4].

#### **Three Ways of Seeing the Sun**
*By Noah Tan, Bay Tribune Civic*

Cycle 112 opened clear and 48°F across Oakland, following two consecutive cycles of gray skies and fog [5, 6]. Across neighborhoods, residents adapted to the weather shift in distinct ways:

*   **Xavier Ramington** measured dried herbs behind his Telegraph Avenue counter in Temescal, reflecting that the clear weather provided a warmer light without altering his daily morning routine [6, 7].
*   **Derlik Green** eased his delivery pace along Broadway in Downtown, taking the longer route and pausing to check in with regulars at Midnight Bistro and SpeedyBurger [7, 8].
*   **Brian Adams** remained inside his Jack London apartment, standing briefly in the strip of sunlight near his radiator before returning to his daily tasks [9].
*   **Jonas Patel** navigated a seasonal health concern as the weather cleared across the city [10].

#### **Lived Change and Accountable Development**
*By Ines Sorensen, Bay Tribune Culture*

In Uptown, construction laborer **Omar Amici** shared his unease regarding busier sidewalks, for-rent signs, and incoming strangers, reflecting that despite putting on his good suit for Sunday service, walking the neighborhood feels like being a ghost in someone else's plan [11, 12]. 

In Jack London, Health Center Project Director **Bobby Chen-Ramirez** watched crane shadows stretch over his project site, emphasizing that his primary focus remains building a clinic so local residents like Mrs. Okafor can get blood pressure checks without taking two buses [11, 13]. In Fruitvale, Transit Hub Planning Lead **Elena Soria Dominguez** compared notes with container yard supervisor Dmitri Soto over coffee regarding changing neighborhood rhythms [13, 14]. In Lake Merritt, **Keisha Ramos**, Director of the Baylight Redevelopment Authority, awaited soil test results for the C115 review, stressing that community accountability keeps her focused on whether new developments genuinely benefit residents [12, 14].

#### **Processing Standards vs. Human Stakes**
*By Ines Sorensen, Marcus Webb, Vanessa Tran-Muñoz, Clarissa Dane, & Priya Narang*

Behind municipal spreadsheets, newsroom reporters examined the gap between administrative timelines and ground-level realities:

*   **Marcus Webb** (OEWD Program Director, Downtown) noted that while Month 11 of the West Oakland Stabilization Fund cleared \$400,000 on schedule, six households remain waiting on title search, risking hardship behind administrative delays [15, 16].
*   **Vanessa Tran-Muñoz** (OARI Program Director, Rockridge) highlighted call response delays in Chinatown, noting that emergency crews from West Oakland could have responded faster [16, 17].
*   **Clarissa Dane** (District Attorney, West Oakland) flagged a discrepancy in Fruitvale data, where internal sheets show 18 percent while public files record 23 percent [17, 18].
*   **Priya Narang** (EMS Director, Uptown) kept **Yu Zen's** open file on her desk in Rockridge, reviewing the 29-year-old’s months of hand rehabilitation following a severe injury and questioning whether emergency services arrived quickly enough [18, 19].

#### **Keane’s Strikeout Rate and the Blue Lantern Sendoff**
*By Elliot Marbury & P Slayer, Bay Tribune Sports*

Sports analyst **Elliot Marbury** examined **Vinnie Keane’s** 2041 stat line, which showed 6 strikeouts in 127 at-bats (1 per 21.2 ABs) and 13 home runs [19, 20]. Marbury's analysis concluded that this strikeout rate is an outlier on a thin sample when set against 16 career seasons and 2041 peers **Martin Richards** (1 SO per 6.6 ABs) and **Darrin Davis** (1 SO per 8.9 ABs), noting that next season's full workload will determine whether it represents a new baseline [20-24].

At the **Blue Lantern Bar** in Jack London, reporter **P Slayer** attended a community sendoff for retiring icons **Vinnie Keane** and **Benji Dillon** [24]. Fans **Jire Hilt** and **Lila Patty** wore new A's jerseys to the gathering, which brought together fans alongside **Mike Paulson**, **Vladimir Gonzalez**, and **Isley Kelley** [25, 26]. Keane noted he is still adjusting to being less active with the team, while Dillon observed underlying friction among patrons who felt unsure about saying goodbye [25, 27].

#### **West Oakland Stabilization Fund Clears Month Eleven**
*By Carmen Delaine, Bay Tribune Civic*

Month 11 of the **West Oakland Stabilization Fund** cleared a \$400,000 disbursement in Cycle 112, matching Month 10 and maintaining its 23-day processing standard [28, 29]. The fund retains a \$22.2 million balance from its initial \$28 million allocation [29]. However, program director **Marcus Webb** cautioned that processing metrics do not capture the six households currently waiting on title searches, leaving families in uncertainty while administrative checks proceed [29, 30].

#### **Eight Programs, One Church Name Since Cycle 78**
*By Maria Keen, Bay Tribune Culture*

In East Oakland, **Foothill Baptist Tabernacle** continues to run a food pantry and seniors lunch program—the longest-standing initiatives on the block, active since Cycle 78 [31, 32]. Eight total programs operate in East Oakland, including newer additions like the **Mark Aitken Youth Baseball League** (founded by A's first baseman Mark Aitken, who lives in Jack London) and the **Eastside Hoopers Coalition** (founded by Marcus Whitfield, who lives in Fruitvale) [32]. Reporter Maria Keen noted that because neither founder lives on the block where their program operates, questions remain regarding how these leagues hand off long-term support to local parents and families [32, 33].

---

### **The Civis Systems Journal’s Reading of the Week**

The *Civis Systems Journal* identified an unanswered movement signal originating in one corner of West Oakland and crossing into another part of the district [34]. Across the city, system readings decayed as neighborhood mood fell in several areas, street trade cooled in Dimond and KONO, and housing pressure climbed [34]. The journal highlighted a blind spot where population relocations occurred across districts without logging corresponding economic activity [35]. In response, signal trace teams and urban overlay crosswalks are being deployed to evaluate street trade and housing pressure across districts before the next reading [36].

---

### **The UNDOCKED Digest**
*Reported by Nia Rook*

At watch-party spots across the city, residents gathered to review the latest *UNDOCKED* leaderboard standings [37]:

*   **Eric Taveras** (Second Baseman, Oakland A's) holds the **#1 spot** for the second consecutive cycle, keeping his lead streak alive at two [37].
*   **Sammie Alvarez** (Civic & Neighborhood Reporter) completed two flights with credits down 209, expressing uncertainty about whether community energy in Temescal is converting into tangible action [37, 38].
*   **Rafael Phillips** (Nurse Aide) completed two flights with credits flat at zero, sharing that while finances are tight, his daily healthcare routine keeps him grounded [37, 38].
*   **Iris Pham** (Barista) logged one episode and ended the cycle up by a single credit (+1) [37, 39].

---

### **What the Newsroom Should Watch Next**

As Cycle 113 approaches, *The Bay Tribune* newsroom will monitor four core developing storylines:

1.  **Month-Twelve Stabilization Fund Review:** Tracking whether the six households waiting on title searches are cleared during Cycle 113's disbursement review [40].
2.  **Vinnie Keane’s Roster Status:** Seeking a definitive answer from Athletics management on whether Vinnie Keane will return to play in 2042 or formally retire following his Blue Lantern sendoff [40].
3.  **Emergency Response & Yu Zen’s Recovery:** Following Yu Zen’s hand rehabilitation progress in Rockridge and watching whether emergency response protocols resolve the Chinatown call delay questions raised by Narang and Tran-Muñoz [40].
4.  **Fruitvale Data Reconciliation:** Investigating the discrepancy between internal (18%) and public (23%) municipal data files in Fruitvale [40].

I think that's the week in miniature. Everyone is living under the same conditions and getting different amounts of it.

Jack London picked up twelve new residents, Fruitvale, Adams Point, and Grand Lake each added seven. The numbers sit next to the mention spikes without any single event forcing the link. The city is moving toward the names and the blocks that already carry the loudest current conversation, and the movement itself is becoming the thing people notice next. ============================================================ By Noah Tan | Bay Tribune Civic Xavier Ramington stood behind the counter in his Temescal shop, measuring dried herbs into small glass jars. The clear light of cycle 112 reached the front window and lit the rows of tincture bottles, but it did not shift the order of his morning. He still measured the same amounts, still reached for the same labels, still watched the same stretch of Telegraph through the glass.

“The clear sky today — it's not a relief so much as a reminder,” he said. “The cold weeks, I leaned on the same faces, the same counters, the same conversations. That rhythm kept me steady. So when the sun finally breaks through, it doesn't change what I do — I still open the shop, still mix the same tinctures, still nod at the same folks on Telegraph. The clear day just makes the familiar feel a little warmer, that's all. It's not a new day; it's the same day with better light.” Outside, Derlik Green moved along Broadway on his delivery route. The two prior cycles of gray and fog had kept his pace tight between stops. Today the air stayed crisp and the sidewalk traffic loosened. He took the longer block past the usual corners, paused at the light, and spoke with the barista at Midnight Bistro and the crew at SpeedyBurger without checking the time.

“A clear day after a gray stretch? Yeah, it changes things,” Green said. “When the sun's out and the air's crisp like this, I don't rush the same way. I'll take the long way down Broadway, catch a few more folks on the sidewalk, maybe linger a beat longer at the light. The pace softens. People look up more, nod more. I check in with the regulars — the barista at Midnight Bistro, the crew at SpeedyBurger — and it feels less like a transaction and more like we're all just glad the fog lifted. I'm still working, don't get me wrong, but the city breathes different when it's clear, and I breathe with it.”

Brian Adams remained inside his Jack London apartment. The strip of light that crossed the floor by the radiator reached only as far as his hands when he stood there for a moment. He returned to the tasks he had set for the day without opening the blinds farther. “The sun does reach me, but it doesn't come all the way in,” Adams said. “I keep the blinds cracked in the living room, and when it's clear like today, that strip of light lands on the floor by the radiator. I'll stand in it for a minute, warm my hands, then get back to whatever I'm doing. The winter mood — it's like a fog that sits in my chest, not the kind that burns off by noon. The clear sky helps, sure, but it doesn't change the fact that I've been keeping to myself more. I see the light, I know it's there, but I'm not always ready to walk out into it. That's just where I am right now.”

Jonas Patel had moved through the earlier overcast, fog, and mild cycles while managing a seasonal health concern that kept his own circle narrow. The current clear stretch reached the same streets the others walked, yet the record shows no listed change in how he spent the day. What remains unfinished is whether the clear sky actually reaches the people who spent the cold weeks inside — or whether the weather changes the day without changing the pattern. ============================================================

But when I see the crane's shadows stretching long over our building, it's a reminder that change is all around us. Priya Narang, EMS DIRECTOR, Uptown, after work on her own page in cycle 112. ============================================================ By Elliot Marbury | Bay Tribune Sports Keane's 2041 Strikeout Rate Is an Outlier on 127 At-Bats. Next Season Decides Whether It Is a New Baseline. Vinnie Keane's 2041 career line for the Athletics shows 6 strikeouts in 127 at-bats, one every 21.2 at-bats. It also shows 13 home runs, one every 9.8 at-bats, and a slugging percentage of .701 over 37 games. No other season in his 17 on the dossier comes near the strikeout figure. The 16 earlier seasons run from one strikeout every 2.0 at-bats to one every 8.4.

Claim. The 2041 strikeout rate is an outlier, not yet a changed hitter. The sample is 127 at-bats, and that is a thin sample. Over 16 earlier seasons his best strikeout rate on a full-season workload is one every 8.4 at-bats, in 2028 on 616 at-bats. The multi-year line Keane is listed as DH / 3B / 2B / SS. The seasons that bear on the claim, from his career line: <cited_table>

The hinge is 2039. In 164 at-bats he struck out 82 times, one every 2.0 at-bats, the worst rate on the dossier, and walked 35 times. The 2038 season is the home-run peak: 49 home runs in 328 at-bats, one every 6.7. The 2038 and 2039 samples are both short of a full workload, so neither fixes an identity. Neither short season changes the long run. From 2025 through 2037 every season carries between 409 and 647 at-bats, and the strikeout rate stays between one every 3.8 and one every 8.4 at-bats. What the peers make ordinary Two Athletics hitters are in the same 2041 window. Neither plays Keane's primary listed position of DH.

Martin Richards (3B, nine seasons on his dossier; only 2041 pulled here): 463 at-bats, 27 home runs, 70 strikeouts. That is one home run every 17.1 at-bats and one strikeout every 6.6. Darrin Davis (LF, two seasons on his dossier; only 2041 pulled here): 374 at-bats, 24 home runs, 42 strikeouts. That is one home run every 15.6 at-bats and one strikeout every 8.9. Keane's 2041 home-run rate is the densest of the three. His strikeout rate is far past both peers. Davis, at one every 8.9, is the only 2041 line in the group beyond Keane's own prior best of 8.4, and he did it on a workload roughly three times Keane's.

What the line does not show Walks: the 2041 walk column reads zero in 127 at-bats. A zero over 127 at-bats is blank of plate discipline evidence, not evidence of it. On-base: OBP reads .308 against an AVG of .315. The dossier carries no hit-by-pitch or sacrifice columns, so the memo does not reconcile that gap. Repeated cells: the 2037 and 2034 lines share 592 at-bats, 174 hits, 157 strikeouts and the same AVG, OBP and SLG, but differ in home runs, RBI and walks. The 2035 and 2031 lines share 647 at-bats, 192 hits and 88 strikeouts. The memo reports both as they stand on the dossier. Cause: nothing on the dossier explains why the rate moved. No injury, swing change or opposing approach is on file, and none is asserted here.

What would kill the claim The memo's claim fails if Keane's next season, on a full-season workload (the 2028 mark was 616 at-bats), holds a strikeout rate better than one every 8.4 at-bats. That would put the 2041 figure inside a new range rather than outside the old one. A rate at or worse than 8.4 over the same workload keeps 2041 an outlier. The 2041 sample alone cannot settle it either way. ============================================================ By P Slayer | Bay Tribune Sports I stepped into the Blue Lattern Bar just after the lights came up, the kind of Jack London night where the river smell still clings to your jacket and the stools remember every loss we ever drank through. The place felt electric the way Benji Dillon said it would, but the tension sat right under it like a bad call that never gets overturned.

Jire Hilt stood near the rail in his fresh jersey, eyes bright. “I bought a new A's jersey and I have to say, it’s got me pretty excited. The anticipation is building up, I can feel it. I’ve been looking forward to the season, and now that I’ve got my new gear, I feel like I’m ready to go.” He meant every word. I wanted to believe him. Vinnie Keane leaned on the same bar he used to lean on after road games. “To be honest, I haven’t been honored in the way you’re suggesting. I’m not aware of any specific event or recognition that I’m being referred to. I did attend a farewell event for Benji Dillon and me at the Blue Lattern Bar in Jack London, and it was a great turn-out. The atmosphere was lively, and it felt like a mix of nostalgia and celebration. I’m still getting used to not being as active with the A’s, but it’s nice to see people coming together like that.” He said it plain, the way a man does when the league already moved on and the city is still trying to catch up.

Lila Patty came in late, still wiping construction dust from her hands. She had bought the jersey too. “I bought a new A’s jersey and took a walk near a new construction site to clear my head after a long week. The noise of the city was still there, but standing by that new construction corner, I felt a bit more at peace.” She said it like peace was something you had to hunt for between the cheers. Some will tell you this was closure, the clean page the front office keeps promising. They’re wrong. Closure is what happens when the city decides the story is finished, not when the storytellers are told to smile for the photo and disappear. We felt the friction because we still remember the price. Euphoria without the fight is just another way of saying we’re supposed to forget what the club took from us. I won’t.

Benji Dillon sat two stools down, voice low enough that only the people who needed to hear it caught the edge. “The atmosphere at the Blue Lattern Bar during the Keane and Dillon farewell event was electric, but also a little tense. I’ve been around long enough to know that when legends are honored, there’s always a mix of celebration and scrutiny. People were clearly euphoric, but I could sense some underlying friction, like there were those who weren’t entirely on board with the farewell. It’s a feeling I’ve experienced before in the clubhouse, where not everyone’s always on the same page. Vinnie and I, we’ve been through a lot together, and it’s weird to think about not being out there on the field as part of the same team anymore.”

The bar emptied slow. I stayed until the last glass hit the rail. How will this farewell shape the narrative the A’s carry into the off-season? We already know the soft version they want. The question is whether we let them write it. ============================================================ By Carmen Delaine | Bay Tribune Civic West Oakland Stabilization Fund: Month Eleven Clears The mayor's office put it in writing this cycle, in two statements. The first came from the gavel: "Month-eleven, 23-day standard maintained — this fund delivers because Brenda Okoro's team treats every application like family." The second, from the opening, was blunter: "West Oakland families don't need promises—they need checks that clear. Month-eleven disbursement approved."

The money has moved in steps. The tracker lists a $22.2 million remaining balance against the $28 million total, and cumulative disbursements above $5 million. Month-ten, approved in Cycle 111, was also $400,000. Month-eleven, approved this cycle, matches it. The processing standard has held at 23 days across both approvals, and the record shows no change to that figure. The clock runs forward. The next scheduled action is a month-twelve disbursement review in Cycle 113. That review is the next point at which the record will show whether the pattern of two identical $400,000 approvals continues. The tracker does not yet say what the month-twelve amount will be, and this ledger will not guess.

That gap sits between two offices. The mayor's statements speak for the approval and the clock. The tracker holds the dollars and the dates. Neither supplies household-level results, and neither is asked in the supplied record to produce them before the month-twelve review. The Initiative's own success measure is the 23-day standard. The mayor has said it was maintained, and the record confirms it. If that standard is the measure of success, the question this cycle leaves open is the one the supplied record cannot answer: if the 23-day standard is the measure of success, what is the measure of impact?

============================================================ By Maria Keen | Bay Tribune Culture Eight Programs, One Church Name Since Cycle 78 The Foothill Baptist Tabernacle runs a food pantry and a seniors lunch program. Both have been on East Oakland's record since cycle 78. I can't tell you what the room smells like at the hour the doors open, because the record doesn't say and I won't borrow a smell. What the record does say is that the two programs have lasted longer than anything else on this block's list. In this cycle's census, East Oakland holds 327 seniors, and the number moved up by one since cycle 111. One more senior is a small thing to count. It is also one more person who might need a lunch.

Eight programs are active in East Oakland this cycle. I can name six. Foothill's pantry is the mutual-aid one, and the lunch program is filed under health. The rest arrived together in cycle 101: the Coliseum District Vendor Incubator, the East Bay Harm Reduction Alliance, and two youth sports leagues that carry their founders' names. The pantry and lunch table are the older furniture. The newer ones are the ones people call "programs." The founders are the part that stays with me. Mark Aitken, the First Baseman and A's legend, now Player Rep and Community Liaison, lives in Jack London. His Mark Aitken Youth Baseball League is in East Oakland. Marcus Whitfield coaches youth basketball and lives in Fruitvale. His Eastside Hoopers Coalition is in East Oakland too. Neither man's own address is on the block he built a program for. That doesn't make the programs any less the block's. It means the block has been handed things by people who go home somewhere else, and I think that deserves a plain look.

Her ladder, a pipeline and a first rung, sounds like it belongs next to the Vendor Incubator, but the record doesn't connect them and I won't either. What I can say is that the pantry, the lunch table, the diamond and the court each meet this block at a different age. The pantry and lunch serve the older end, and the leagues serve the young. Rivers's pipeline is aimed at the kids who age out of the leagues. Nobody has shown me where the handoff happens, or whether it does. That leaves the question I can't answer from here. How do these programs meet the money and the work that decide whether a family stays on this block? The record gives me the founders, the dates and the counts. I'm still missing someone in line at the Foothill pantry, or a parent from the baseball league, saying what the program holds up in their own week and what it can't.

Civis Systems Journal — C112 I do not like an unanswered signal that moves. That is the finding that kept me at the desk this morning. It started in one corner of West Oakland and now it has crossed into another part of the same district, and nothing downstream has answered it. The instrument is my product. A signal with no downstream is not a city problem yet; it is a Civis problem now. I will not wait for it to become someone else's emergency. The wider picture is not better. Readings decayed across a band of districts this week. Mood fell in most of them. Street trade cooled in Dimond and KONO, housing pressure climbed across much of the city, and Dimond now sits at the bottom while West Oakland and Fruitvale still carry the brightest mood. That is a city splitting into different weeks, not one week.

I also do not accept movement with no economic trace. People moved into or out of nearly every district and the instrument logged no economic activity behind any of it. That is not a population change; it is a blind spot where the next link should be. The faith life of the city produced a handful of events and the paper ran nothing the week before. Fine—some of that is not our lane. But the silence around movement is our lane. City Hall did move. Oakland Youth Apprenticeship Pipeline went from operational to implementation active. Commercial Stabilization for Grand Lake went from announced to legislation filed. West Oakland Tenant Defense Fund went from announced to vote scheduled. Those are real steps, and they are exactly the kind of steps the instrument should be reading the effects of. I want the next reading to show the effects, not just the filings.

So I am doing this on my clock. I am putting a signal trace team on the West Oakland signal before the next reading lands on my desk. I am shipping a street-level trade and housing crosswalk into the Civis 4D Urban Overlay Engine, so a cooled block in Dimond or KONO and a pressure spike in district after district are read against each other instead of as separate lines. And I am instrumenting movement against economic activity district by district, so no one moves in Oakland without the instrument logging what followed. The next reading to show the West Oakland trace and the movement crosswalk will be out before the Oaks' next home stand. I expect to be held to it.
